newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives fight back on unions, economy.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives fight back on unions, economy.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative Party, striving to regain the election initiative, warned on Monday that plans by its Labour opponents to increase the rights of trade unions risked wrecking a thriving economy.

After a stumbling first week's campaigning for the May 1 election, top Conservatives seized on Labour's intention to include long-held plans for union recognition in a manifesto it is drafting to underscore their own pro-business credentials.

"As Britain's businesses plan for continued success in our booming economy, Labour's proposals for new union power would put that success at risk. The message is clear: don't let Labour blow it," Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said.
Under the main opposition party's plans, companies would be required by law to recognise and negotiate with a union if more than 50 percent of the staff voted to join it.
Moderate Labour leader Tony Blair has said he would not reverse the bulk of the sweeping anti-union reforms pushed through during the last 18 years of Conservative rule.
He has promised the unions fairness, not favours.

But Conservatives said Blair's recognition policy showed Labour was in the pocket of the unions, which still provide about half of the party's funding even though their influence in policy-making has been sharply curtailed in recent years.

"The revelation that Labour's business manifesto will include new privileges for the trade unions is clear confirmation that union interests would hold sway under any Labour government," Heseltine told a news conference.
He said the plan was "damaging and dangerous" because it could put Britain's much-improved labour relations under strain and give unions huge scope to interfere in how firms are run.
Labour holds a poll lead of about 25 percentage points but surveys also show voters are nervous about a resurgence of union power if it takes office for the first time since 1979.

Labour's trade and industry spokeswoman, Margaret Beckett, stressed that unions would win the right to negotiate with employers on issues such as pay and hours only if more than half the workforce wanted to be represented.
"What's wrong about people having the right to belong to a union and having the right to be represented by it if a majority of them want to be?" Beckett asked on BBC radio.
Prime Minister John Major was glad to put the focus on the economy after last week's start to the campaign became bogged down in damaging allegations of sleaze in the ruling party.

Following good unemployment, inflation and government borrowing figures last week, news on Monday that Britain's balance of payments was virtually in balance last year provided further evidence of economic strength.

"Britain is booming thanks to people's hard work and Conservative policies. This is prosperity built to last, backed by sustainable growth," he said in a statement during a campaign tour of marginal constituencies in western England.
But Labour and the centre-left Liberal Democrats pointed to a warning by Oxford Economic Forecasting, a respected consulting firm, that inflation would rise and growth slow later this year.
Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown said economic boom would inevitably be followed by bust, and attacked Labour for blindly copying the Conservatives' economic policies.

"I greatly fear that the Conservatives with the consent of Labour have now decided to engineer a temporary pre-election mini-boom to get themselves elected and will invite people once again to pay with higher interest rates, higher inflation and higher mortgages after the election," he said.
